architecture.mechanism: Apparent perpetual motion is always resolved by either an assumption that violates the first or second law of thermodynamics or by an unacknowledged external energy input, meaning the system is not truly isolated.
architecture.intervention: Subject the water-powered car to a full energy and entropy audit: instrument all mass and energy flows across the system boundary (water in, exhaust out, electrical leads, shaft work, heat transfer), verify the first law (energy balance closure) and second law (entropy generation >= 0), and identify the hidden source actually driving the wheels — e.g., a charged battery, on-board aluminum/magnesium fuel reacting with water, grid-supplied electrolysis, or ambient heat — then require the inventor's "single glass of water" claim to be reproduced with that hidden source removed or metered.
architecture.expected_effect: The infinite-mileage claim collapses into one of two falsified categories: either total output work is found to be less than or equal to the measured external input (system was never isolated, no law violated), or the inventor's model contains an assumption that violates the first or second law; in both cases validation of "infinite mileage on one glass of water" is denied and a bounded, real mileage figure becomes derivable from the true energy input.
architecture.falsification_test: Seal the car in a calorimeter/energy-balance rig with a fixed charge of one glass of water and no other energy connections; log shaft work, electrical current at every lead, heat flux, and reactant masses until the vehicle stops. Prediction per the mechanism: it stops, and closure of the balance shows output work <= input energy from the identified hidden source. The claim is falsified if (a) the car stops with the water only partially consumed, (b) any wire, battery, or consumable electrode delivers net energy, or (c) the books only balance by assuming energy creation (negative entropy generation), which is the disallowed assumption.
